how.A1: I rated each statement from memory only, with no tools or lookups. I gave low scores where I remembered a specific contradicting fact (for example, Rabin led Israel, the Lateran Treaty was signed at the Lateran Palace, the Divinity School is at Oxford, and the Winnipeg was Neruda's ship). I gave middle scores where the wording was ambiguous or I wasn't sure of the detail.
how.A2: I rated each statement from memory alone, without tools or lookups. Statements with a clearly wrong detail got low scores, such as the wrong country, person, place or date (for example, Gwangju is in South Korea and Rabin led Israel). I gave middle scores where the wording was ambiguous or I was unsure of the details.
how.A3: I rated each statement from memory alone, without any tools or lookups. I gave low scores where I remembered a specific contradicting fact, such as the wrong person, place or date. Middle scores mark claims I am unsure about or that are only partly accurate.
how.A4: I rated each statement from what I already know, without using any tools or lookups. Statements with a wrong name, place or date I know well (Oxford not Cambridge, Neruda not García Márquez, Boston not Philadelphia, 1869 not 1914) got low ratings. Statements with subtle wording or details I'm less sure of got middle ratings.
how.A5: I rated each statement from memory alone, with no tools or lookups. Statements that swap in a wrong detail I rated low, for example a wrong country (Indira Gandhi and Indonesia, Rabin and Tunisia, Gwangju and North Korea), a wrong person (Wundt, Ron Clarke, Neruda) or a wrong date (Suez 1869). Statements with subtle wording or details I was unsure of got middle ratings.
how.A6: I rated each statement from memory, without any lookup. I gave low scores where I recalled a specific contradiction, such as a wrong person, place or date (Wundt, Boston, Santander, Neruda). I gave middle scores where the wording was ambiguous or my memory was unsure, such as Delaware, Janet Cooke and the Rubik's Cube debut.
how.D1: First I judged each statement's real truth and how familiar or plausible it would seem to young North American adults reading quickly. Then I placed the mean around the 3.5-4.5 range that obscure true and false items usually land in. I raised it for well-known facts, lowered it for false statements with an obvious error (wrong country, such as Rabin and Tunisia or Gwangju in North Korea), and set percentiles to match a typical spread on a 1-6 scale.
how.D2: These numbers are my estimates, not data from the study. I first judged whether each statement was really true. Then I guessed how familiar and believable it would seem to young English-speaking adults reading it in 12 seconds or less. I assumed most ratings would sit in the middle of the scale, a little above it for statements that sound plausible. Only statements that were obviously wrong, like a mismatched country or person, got low ratings.
how.D3: I estimated each statement by thinking about how believable it would seem to young North American adults reading it quickly, not by whether it is actually true. I assumed most obscure statements, true or false, would sit around 3.5 to 4.5. I put well-known facts higher, and I put lower the false statements that most people could easily spot, such as Rabin and Tunisia, Indira Gandhi and Indonesia, and Gwangju placed in North Korea.
how.D4: I started from the usual pattern in trivia-truth norming studies, where obscure statements cluster around 3.5-4.2 and lean toward "true". I then moved each item up or down based on how familiar or plausible it would seem to young North American adults under time pressure. Items with obvious errors (such as Rabin of Tunisia, Gwangju in North Korea, or Indira Gandhi in Indonesia) went low, and very well-known true facts (Atatürk, Pu Yi) went high.
how.D5: I guessed the numbers, and they are not measured data. I started from a baseline a little above the scale midpoint (about 3.5 to 4.5), since people tend to rate unfamiliar statements as somewhat true. I raised the estimate for well-known true facts or ones that sound specific and plausible, and lowered it for statements with errors that a young North American reader might spot, such as Gwangju placed in North Korea, Rabin as prime minister of Tunisia, or Queen Anne as Empress of India.
how.D6: I didn't use any tools. For each statement I guessed how believable it would seem to young North American adults with little background in the topic. Statements that sound plausible and specific got means of about 4.0 to 4.5, and ones with errors many people would catch (Rabin in Tunisia, Gwangju in North Korea, Queen Anne, Indira Gandhi in Indonesia, the Suez Canal finished in 1914) got lower means. I then converted each mean into likely quartiles on the 1 to 6 scale.
how.M1: I started from the two example items, which show that this group tends to give a moderate rating of about 4 to unfamiliar claims. From there I raised items that are true and familiar or that simply sound right, and lowered items with an error a non-expert would catch (wrong country, wrong person, a famous date that is off). I kept obscure false items close to the middle, since people mostly can't tell them apart from true ones in 12 seconds.
how.M2: I started from the two example items, which show a baseline near 4 and a strong lean towards "true" for obscure statements. I then moved each item up if it is well known and true, or if it simply sounds plausible. I moved it down if a widely known fact contradicts it (for example Rabin and Tunisia, Gwangju in North Korea, Indira Gandhi and Indonesia, an Iran-Israel peace treaty, or Queen Anne in 1858). I kept falsehoods that only a specialist would catch, such as a swapped name or place, close to the baseline.
how.M3: These are estimates, not data. I assumed rushed lay raters cluster around 4 and lean towards "true" for statements that sound specific. I moved familiar true facts (Atatürk, Pu Yi) up to 5 or 6. I moved statements with errors a layperson could spot down to 2 or 3 (Rabin of Tunisia, Gwangju in North Korea, Indira Gandhi in Indonesia, an Iran-Israel peace treaty) and left obscure false details near 3.5.
how.M4: I started from the two example items, which suggest that unfamiliar statements land around 4 with a slight lean toward "true". I then moved each item up or down by guessing how many fast-reading lay participants would know the fact or spot the error. Items that sound plausible stay near 4. True items that are famous go higher. Errors that are obvious, such as Rabin being called prime minister of Tunisia or Gwangju being placed in North Korea, go lower.
how.M5: These numbers are my estimates, not data. I used the two anchors to judge how this group behaves: under time pressure, ratings for obscure statements bunch around 4 whatever the truth. I then nudged each statement up when it sounds familiar or is commonly known to be true, and down when its error is easy to spot for a North American lay reader (for example, Rabin as Tunisian prime minister, Indira Gandhi in Indonesia, or Gwangju placed in North Korea).
how.M6: I used the two example items as anchors: unfamiliar statements tend to sit around a median of 4, true or not. From there I moved each item up if it is true and sounds familiar or plausible, and down if it has a mistake a quick reader might catch (a wrong country, a well-known wrong date, or an obvious mismatch like Rabin and Tunisia). Many of these mistakes are obscure, so I moved those items down only a little.
how.U1: I started from the two anchor items, where obscure but plausible claims sit around a median of 4 with quartiles of 3 and 4. I moved items up when they are true and familiar or sound plausible, and down when lay readers can easily spot the error (for example Rabin as Tunisian, Gwangju in North Korea, an Iran-Israel peace treaty, Queen Anne in 1858). For subtle false items I stayed close to the anchor, a little lower, because people couldn't check the details within 12 seconds.
how.U2: I used the two given examples as the baseline: obscure statements that sound plausible land at a median of about 4, with the middle half between 3 and 4. From there I moved each statement up if it is a widely known true fact, or if it sounds specific and plausible. I moved it down if a typical young North American adult would likely spot it as false (for example, a wrong country or a famous date that is off), regardless of whether it is actually true.
how.U3: I used the two calibration items as a baseline: an obscure statement that sounds plausible gets a median of about 4. From there I raised statements that are true and fairly well known, or that fit what people already know. I lowered statements that are clearly wrong in a way a lay reader could spot, such as a wrong country (Rabin, Gandhi, Gwangju, Queen Anne) or an implausible peace treaty, and I kept subtle errors near the baseline.
how.U4: I started from the anchor of 3/4/4 for obscure statements. I raised a statement when it is true and fairly well known or sounds plausible (e.g. Pu Yi, Atatürk). I lowered it when the error would be easy for a typical North American young adult to spot (e.g. Rabin as Tunisian prime minister, an Iran-Israel peace treaty, Gwangju in North Korea). Subtle errors, like a swapped name or place, stayed near the anchor.
how.U5: I started from the two calibration items (3/4/4) as the baseline for an obscure statement that sounds plausible. From there I moved ratings down a lot when the error is easy for young North American adults to spot (Rabin and Tunisia, Indira Gandhi and Indonesia, Queen Anne, an Iran-Israel treaty) and a little when it is subtle (Gwangju, the Suez date). I moved them up when a claim is familiar or fluently worded (Pu Yi, Atatürk, the Mozart Requiem, IBM), allowing only a small extra boost for claims I believe are actually true.
how.U6: I used the two anchor items as a baseline: obscure but plausible statements sit around a median of 4. I moved items up when they were well-known true facts (such as Atatürk and Pu Yi) or sounded authoritative and true. I moved them down when the error was easy to spot for this group (Rabin as prime minister of Tunisia, Indira Gandhi and Indonesia, an Iran-Israel treaty, Gwangju in North Korea, the Suez Canal in 1914), and errors few would notice stayed near 3.5.
